name: Haleakalā National Park
tagline: A summit above the clouds and a rainforest coast of waterfalls on Maui.

photo.alt: Low clouds hang in the expansive crater, surrounded by hills under a clear sky
photo.caption: Haleakala Crater from the Halemau'u Trail

intro: Haleakalā rises 10,023 feet above Maui, and from its summit the vast crater, its cinder cones and the Pacific spread out below. Far down the mountain's southeast flank, the Kīpahulu District is a world of streams, bamboo and waterfalls on the coast near Hāna. Haleakalā is sacred to Native Hawaiians, and the park names a small number of summit and coastal places where a family may scatter ashes with a permit.
scatterSummary: Scattering is permitted with a special use permit, only at six approved summit and Kīpahulu locations.
scatterFacts: Permit: NPS Form 10-930 for scattering of ashes, with a copy of the death certificate and a non-refundable $25 application fee. Email hale_commercial_manager@nps.gov (preferred). Apply at least three weeks ahead; complex requests need at least four weeks. Entrance fees still apply.
Approved summit sites: Puʻuʻulaʻula (Red Hill), Pā Kaʻoao Overlook (White Hill), Kalahaku Overlook and Leleiwi Overlook.
Approved Kīpahulu sites: the Kūloa Loop Trail and the Coastal Trail from Kūloa Point to Kīpahulu Campground.
Not approved: the Wilderness Area (including wilderness cabins and campgrounds) and the Kaʻapahu and Alelele areas. No off-trail access. Groups of 25 or fewer.

Plan a small private affair away from high visitor use areas; other visitors are not excluded. Ashes must not be identifiable as human remains. Plants, flowers or lei must leave the park with you, and no memorials, plaques or photos may be left.
A permit for sunrise hours also requires a sunrise reservation from Recreation.gov.

scatterLink.label: Special use permits: scattering of ashes (NPS)

beforeYouGo: The two districts are not connected by road. Summit District: from Kahului by Routes 37, 377 and 378 (about 2.5 hours to the summit); the entrance-to-summit drive takes about 30 minutes, with no streetlights or guard rails. The summit is always open, but entry from 3 am to 7 am requires a sunrise reservation ($1 per vehicle, Recreation.gov, up to 60 days ahead). Kīpahulu District: Routes 36, 360 and 31, 12 miles past Hāna (about 4 hours from Kahului). No gas or food in the park. At 10,000 feet expect thin air, freezing wind and strong sun; anyone with heart or breathing conditions should ask a doctor first.

destinations.name: Puʻuʻulaʻula Summit
destinations.description: At 10,023 feet, Puʻuʻulaʻula is the highest point on Maui, and on a clear day the view turns all the way around: the crater, the West Maui Mountains, the neighboring islands and the open Pacific. Many families come up in the dark to watch the sun rise over the crater rim, wrapped in blankets beside the summit building's wide windows. Look for the silvery ʻāhinahina growing nowhere else on earth. This is one of the park's approved scattering sites, a farewell above the clouds.

plan.distance: At the summit parking area; short paved and unpaved paths
plan.accessibility: Wheelchair accessible (NPS); the summit building shelters you from the wind
plan.bestTime: Sunrise (reservation required for entry from 3 am to 7 am) or a clear day

drive.route: Routes 37, 377 and 378 from Kahului to the park entrance, then Crater Road to its end at the summit. Parking is very limited and lots close when full.

scatterNote.text: Stay on the established paths and keep clear of the silverswords. The observatories on the adjacent hill are not part of the park.

destinations.name: Pā Kaʻoao (White Hill)
destinations.description: Right beside the Haleakalā Visitor Center, a short trail climbs a pale cinder hill past the stone walls of ancient rock shelters, part of the mountain's long human history. From the top the crater opens in front of you, its colored cinder cones far below. It is a short walk with a big reward, and an approved scattering site, so the climb, the view and the farewell can all fit into a single unhurried hour together.

plan.accessibility: Rocky trail with stone steps; not wheelchair accessible

drive.route: Routes 37, 377 and 378 to the park, then Crater Road to the Haleakalā Visitor Center parking lot.

trail.name: Pā Kaʻoao Trail
steps: Start beside the Haleakalā Visitor Center.
Climb the cinder hill past the ancient rock wall shelters to the viewpoint over the crater.
notes: Stay on the trail; off-trail travel is not permitted. Leave rocks and cultural structures undisturbed.

destinations.name: Keoneheʻeheʻe (Sliding Sands) Trail

photo.alt: A straight, sandy trail is a cleared path through low vegetation on the flat crater bottom

destinations.description: From the rim, a cinder trail built by the Civilian Conservation Corps in 1937 drops into a crater about 7.5 miles long, with fourteen multicolored cinder cones scattered across its floor. Even the first quarter mile brings a sweeping view, and every step farther down feels more like walking on another planet. Hawaiians crossed this crater for centuries, and following them for a while, together and in quiet, can be a deeply moving way to honor someone who loved wide-open places.

plan.distance: First overlook 0.5 mi round trip; crater floor 3.9 mi one way
plan.difficulty: Moderate for the first mile (NPS); summit trails are strenuous at this altitude
plan.time: About 1 hour for the first mile down and back; allow twice as long to climb out as to go down
plan.elevation: 50 ft to the first overlook; almost 2,500 ft to the crater floor (another NPS page gives about 3,000 ft)
plan.accessibility: Not wheelchair accessible: the first quarter mile is rocky but flat, then steep loose cinder
plan.scattering: Not on this trail (Wilderness Area). See below.

drive.route: Routes 37, 377 and 378 to the park, then Crater Road to the Haleakalā Visitor Center parking lot. The trailhead is in the lot, near the road.

trail.name: Keoneheʻeheʻe (Sliding Sands) Trail
steps: From the trailhead, walk 0.25 mi on a rocky but flat stretch to the Keoneheʻeheʻe Wayside Overlook.
Beyond it the trail descends steeply on loose cinder toward the crater floor, 3.9 mi down.
Turn around whenever you choose; the climb back up takes about twice as long as the descent.
notes: Bring sun protection, warm and wet-weather layers, food and water. Watch for altitude sickness: nausea, headache, dizziness, shortness of breath.
Hiking groups are limited to 12 people; stay on the trail.

final.label: Trailhead (the first overlook is 0.25 mi down the trail)

scatterNote.text: The trail lies in the Wilderness Area, where the park does not approve scattering. Two approved sites are steps away: Pā Kaʻoao beside the visitor center and Puʻuʻulaʻula at the summit. Permit required.

destinations.name: Kūloa Point Trail

photo.alt: Waves breaking on the rocky shore below the Kuloa Point Trail

destinations.description: On the green, rain-washed coast past Hāna, a short trail leaves the Kīpahulu Visitor Center, passes a Hawaiian cultural demonstration area and ends at Kūloa Point, where ʻOheʻo Gulch meets the sea. Below you lie the Pools of ʻOheʻo, and beyond them the ocean stretches away to the horizon. It is a gentle walk for nearly any family, and the park approves this trail for scattering, so you can stand together by the water and say goodbye in a place of quiet, lasting beauty.

plan.accessibility: Short trail; surface details not published
plan.scattering: Allowed on this trail with a permit

drive.route: Routes 36, 360 and 31 (the Hāna Highway) to the Kīpahulu District, 12 miles past Hāna, about 4 hours from Kahului. Last gas before Hāna is in Pāʻia.

trail.name: Kūloa Point Trail
steps: Leave the Kīpahulu Visitor Center and pass the Hawaiian cultural demonstration area.
Continue to Kūloa Point at the mouth of ʻOheʻo Gulch, with views of the pools and the ocean.
notes: The Pools of ʻOheʻo are closed to entry; view them from the trail. Flash floods and rock falls can happen at any time.
Archaeological sites line the trail: leave rocks, artifacts and structures undisturbed, and stay on the trail.

scatterNote.text: Approved along the Kūloa Loop Trail and the Coastal Trail from Kūloa Point to Kīpahulu Campground, on the trail only (no off-trail access). Permit required.

destinations.name: Pīpīwai Trail to Waimoku Falls

photo.alt: Several white waterfalls cascade over an edge 400 feet high and the cliffs are covered in dense, verdant vegetation

destinations.description: The Pīpīwai Trail climbs beside a freshwater stream into a forest that keeps changing as you go. Makahiku Falls appears first, then boardwalks lead into a bamboo forest where the park invites you to listen to the music of the bamboo. At the end, Waimoku Falls drops 400 feet down a sheer green wall. Walking it together, with time to stop and listen, makes a memorable journey for a family, and the falls are a powerful place to share what your loved one meant to you.

plan.difficulty: Moderate (the park calls it moderately strenuous)
plan.accessibility: Boardwalks and footbridges; muddy and slippery in rain

drive.route: Routes 36, 360 and 31 (the Hāna Highway) to the Kīpahulu District, 12 miles past Hāna. The trail starts near the Kīpahulu Visitor Center.

trail.name: Pīpīwai Trail
steps: At 0.5 mi, Makahiku Overlook gives the first view of Makahiku Falls.
At about 1 mi, boardwalks and footbridges lead through the bamboo forest.
At 2 mi the trail ends at the Waimoku Falls viewing area.
notes: Check and obey posted trail closures; off-trail travel is dangerous and illegal.
Wading in the streams is not recommended: flash floods and rock falls can occur at any time.

scatterNote.text: The Pīpīwai Trail is not an approved scattering site. Nearby, the park approves the Kūloa Loop Trail and the Coastal Trail from Kūloa Point to Kīpahulu Campground. Permit required.
